In the engineering hostel, Imran had stopped going to the mess for breakfast. Most mornings he lay on the top bunk, scrolling, feeling flat and heavy while assignments piled up. At noon Himani from the next wing found him in the common room. "Walk to the tea stall with me? Ten minutes, that's all."
He went, grumbling. The sun on the path felt oddly nice. Back in his room, he finished half a problem set.
The next morning he planned a big fix: gym at six, a long run daily, no excuses. He managed one day, then slept through the alarm and felt worse than before.
Himani shook her head. "Forget the gym plan. Just the tea stall walk. Every day, even on bad days. And if the flatness hangs on, the campus counsellor is there too."
So that's what he does. It doesn't fix everything, but most days his head feels a little clearer afterwards.

qa.a: Himani invited Imran to walk to the tea stall.

qa.a: Imran felt worse than before, discouraged after managing only one day.

qa.a: A short daily walk is easier to keep as a gentle habit than an all-or-nothing plan that ends in failure.

qa.a: Himani likely feels quietly pleased, seeing that the small walk helps Imran more than the big plan did.

grounding: A young adult feeling flat finds that a short daily walk lifts energy and thinking a little, as a gentle habit rather than an all-or-nothing plan.

passage:
Dear Maria,
Since you asked how I've been since the placement rejections: flat, mostly. For a few weeks I barely left my room. Then my roommate dragged me out for a walk along the Kochi seafront, and I noticed my head felt a bit less foggy afterwards.
So I've kept it up. Twenty minutes every evening, no targets, no tracking. At first I turned it into a punishment: walk faster, you lazy idiot. That made me hate it. Now I walk slowly on bad days and let that count too. Some days it's just to the ferry and back.
It hasn't turned my life around. But I'm sleeping better, and I've started applying again. Small and regular seems to beat big and occasional.
Write soon,
Divyansh

passage: Since failing her accounts paper, Aparna had felt like wet cardboard. She went to her classes in the Delhi PG, came back, lay on the bed and scrolled until two. Her roommate Rehana didn't lecture her. One evening she just said, 'I'm walking to the chai stall. Ten minutes. Come if you want.' Aparna went, mostly so she wouldn't have to say no. The air was cool, and the stall owner's radio was playing old songs. It didn't fix anything. But on the way back, Aparna noticed she'd thought about the re-exam without dread for the first time in a week. They made it a habit: chai walk after dinner, most days. On the nights Aparna skipped it, Rehana just said, 'Tomorrow, then.' By the end of the month, Aparna had started planning her revision again.

'Bhaiya, it's seven. Weren't you going to the gym at five?'
'I didn't go, Shreya. I didn't go yesterday either.' Sumit pulled the blanket over his head. 'I'm useless.'
'Why five in the morning, though? You hate mornings.'
'Because if I'm going to fix myself, I have to do it properly. Gym every day. No excuses.'
'And now you feel worse because you missed it.'
A muffled grunt.
Shreya sat on the edge of his bed. 'Ever since the job rejections, you've been so low. What if it's not a big plan? What if we just walk to the park after dinner? Fifteen minutes. Some days you won't want to, and that's fine.'
'That's too small to help.'
'Try it for a week.'
A week later, Sumit said, 'The walk's the only part of my day I don't dread.'

passage: Second year was the grey year for me. Nothing terrible happened. I just felt flat: slow in the mornings, foggy in lectures, stressed about everything and interested in nothing. I'm Shalini, and back then my idea of exercise was a huge plan I'd never start. My friend Keerthana had a different idea. 'Just walk round the campus with me after lunch. One loop.' I thought it was pointless. But I went, mostly because she'd wait outside my hostel. One loop took twelve minutes. Some days we talked, some days we didn't. Slowly I noticed the afternoon fog lifted a little after the walk. My notes got clearer. It didn't make the grey year sunny. It made it lighter. I still walk that loop when things feel heavy.

qa.a: Twelve minutes.

qa.a: Shalini felt flat, foggy and stressed, interested in nothing.

qa.a: They were short and regular, not a big plan, and Keerthana's company made it easy to keep going.

qa.a: Keerthana probably felt caring and patient, hoping the small walk would help a friend.

grounding: Shows a young adult in a flat, stressed patch finding that a short daily walk lifts energy and thinking slightly, kept up as a gentle habit.

passage: Counselling notes, Thursday. Jomon came in for his third session looking less grey around the eyes. Two weeks ago he told me he had stopped going to lectures and felt "flat, like a phone on two percent". He had tried a plan of running five kilometres every morning, gave up on day two, and called himself useless. I suggested something much smaller: a ten-minute walk to the tea stall behind the library, every day, no targets. Today he said he has missed only one day. He still feels low most evenings, but says his head is clearer before the afternoon lab, and he laughed while describing a stray dog that now waits for him at the gate. When he mentioned adding push-ups as punishment for any skipped day, I asked him to keep the walk kind instead. Next session in two weeks. Joseph, student counsellor
